account: Between September 2022 and February 2023, archaeologists surveyed the Nazca Pampa in Peru. The sources give only the months of the survey. Masato Sakai of Yamagata University's Institute of Nasca led the team. They used candidate locations proposed by a deep-learning model developed with IBM Research. The model screened aerial photographs at 10-centimeter resolution over more than 600 square kilometers. Field verification confirmed 303 previously unknown figurative relief-type geoglyphs, almost doubling the known total. The model individually suggested 178 of them. The other 125 were found during the AI-guided survey without an individual suggestion. The team screened about 36 AI suggestions per promising candidate. With high-resolution imagery but without AI, discoveries had run at 18.7 a year from 2004 to 2020. The authors report a sixteen-fold increase in the discovery rate. The results appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on 23 September 2024. Johny Isla, Peru's chief archaeologist for the Nazca Lines, told The Guardian on 26 September 2024 that the new figures were too small for past overflights to have detected. Amina Jambajantsan of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, who was not involved, told CNN that doubling the known geoglyphs with limited training data was amazing. She added that AI models are not yet perfectly accurate. On 14 August 2025, The Art Newspaper reported that the same Yamagata University and IBM team had announced 248 further AI-assisted geoglyph finds at Expo 2025 Osaka. This brought the total to 893, of which 781 came from AI and aerial-image analysis.

ai_role.statement: The model proposed candidate locations that directed fieldwork. 178 of the 303 confirmed geoglyphs were individually suggested by the AI. Of the remaining 125, 66 were found as part of an AI-discovered group. The other 59 were found without any help from AI or in screening outside the AI-suggested boxes. Confirmation was by ground survey, not by the model.

fields.account: Between September 2022 and February 2023, archaeologists surveyed the Nazca Pampa in Peru. The sources give only the months of the survey. Masato Sakai of Yamagata University's Institute of Nasca led the team. They used candidate locations proposed by a deep-learning model developed with IBM Research. The model screened aerial photographs at 10-centimeter resolution over more than 600 square kilometers. Field verification confirmed 303 previously unknown figurative relief-type geoglyphs, almost doubling the known total. The model individually suggested 178 of them. The other 125 were found during the AI-guided survey without an individual suggestion. The team screened about 36 AI suggestions per promising candidate. With high-resolution imagery but without AI, discoveries had run at 18.7 a year from 2004 to 2020. The authors report a sixteen-fold increase in the discovery rate. The results appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on 23 September 2024. Johny Isla, Peru's chief archaeologist for the Nazca Lines, told The Guardian on 26 September 2024 that the new figures were too small for past overflights to have detected. Amina Jambajantsan of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, who was not involved, told CNN that doubling the known geoglyphs with limited training data was amazing. She added that AI models are not yet perfectly accurate. On 14 August 2025, The Art Newspaper reported that the same Yamagata University and IBM team had announced 248 further AI-assisted geoglyph finds at Expo 2025 Osaka. This brought the total to 893, of which 781 came from AI and aerial-image analysis.
fields.summary: A deep-learning model from IBM Research and Yamagata University flagged likely sites in aerial photographs, and fieldwork in Peru confirmed 303 new Nazca geoglyphs.

purpose: Built to flag candidate geoglyph locations in aerial imagery so that archaeologists could prioritize ground survey; the discoveries were that purpose.

ratings.reason: Yamagata University's Institute of Nasca reports a sixteen-fold increase in the discovery rate. The German Aerospace Center says that the survey achieved in six months what had previously taken decades.
